oil.summary: Crude markets posted modest daily losses — WTI off 1.15% to $75.01, Brent down 0.82% to $78.89 — but the headline story is RBOB gasoline cratering 9.25% on the day and nearly 24% on the week, a striking divergence from crude. The geopolitical backdrop remains intensely bullish on supply risk: Houthis claimed hits on eight Saudi tankers and an India-flagged vessel carrying Saudi oil reportedly sank off Yemen, while Iran's oil blockade remains in force with Trump threatening further escalation. Saudi Aramco Q2 profits are reported soaring on the Iran war supply squeeze, and a global refining boom is said to be underway. Partially offsetting: EIA data showed a 2.5 million barrel build in US crude inventories for the week ending July 31, and options markets imply a 77% probability of an OPEC cut at the next meeting, signalling demand anxiety beneath the supply-risk narrative.
drivers: Active Houthi attacks on Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, including one confirmed sinking, sustaining severe shipping risk premium
Iran oil blockade ongoing; US-Iran Hormuz deal talks reportedly targeting a Wednesday announcement, creating headline risk in both directions
RBOB gasoline collapsed 9.25% on the day (-23.8% on the week) despite crude holding, pointing to demand destruction or crack spread unwinding; US crude stocks built 2.5 mb

gas.summary: Natural gas price action was split sharply by geography. Henry Hub slipped a modest 0.63% to $2.665/MMBtu, extending a steep one-month decline of over 18%, suggesting continued softness in US domestic fundamentals. TTF in Europe, by contrast, shed a sharp 6.65% on the day to €52.2/MWh, though it remains up 12% on the month — implying European markets had run hard on Middle East supply fears and are now partially pricing in diplomacy: reports indicate the US is targeting a Wednesday announcement on an interim Strait of Hormuz deal. Separately, a senior Syrian official flagged that an Iraq-Syria pipeline bypassing Hormuz could be revived within three years, offering a medium-term alternative routing narrative. Headlines specific to gas supply fundamentals are thin today beyond the Hormuz-linked items.
drivers: US targeting a Wednesday announcement on an interim Strait of Hormuz deal, driving TTF to give back recent geopolitical risk premium (-6.65% on the day)
Iraq-Syria pipeline bypass of Hormuz flagged as potentially operational within three years, offering a structural medium-term supply rerouting option
Henry Hub remains under pressure (-18.4% on the month), reflecting weak US domestic fundamentals independent of Middle East developments

power.summary: The power and carbon complex offered limited fresh catalysts today. EU carbon EUAs edged up 0.42% to $77.14/EUA, roughly flat on the week and month, suggesting the market is in a holding pattern. TTF's sharp 6.65% daily drop is the most relevant input: cheaper gas, if sustained, typically softens short-run marginal costs for gas-fired generation and reduces demand for EUAs, though the relationship has not yet manifested in today's carbon price. China's State Grid Corporation reported electricity demand hitting all-time highs this week amid an intense summer heatwave, a noteworthy demand signal but one with limited direct EUA transmission. A US Senate sanctions push reportedly targeting Russian energy financing and China exposure adds a geopolitical overlay but with no quantifiable near-term power market impact visible in today's data.
drivers: TTF dropped 6.65% on Hormuz deal optimism, which if sustained would ease European gas-fired generation costs and potentially pressure EUA demand
China electricity demand hit record highs this week due to extreme heatwave conditions, per State Grid Corporation — a significant demand signal
EU EUAs broadly flat (+0.42% day, -0.5% month); US Senate sanctions push targeting Russian energy financing adds background geopolitical noise without clear near-term price catalyst
